h: Real rocks right outside the door
p: Here's the clever bit about Dynamic Earth's location. Step outside and you're standing next to some of the most important rocks in the history of science. James Hutton, the Edinburgh thinker often called the father of modern geology, studied the landscape of Holyrood Park in the 18th century, and on Salisbury Crags you can still find Hutton's Section, a rock exposure that helped him work out just how ancient the Earth must be. After a visit that whizzes you through billions of years, standing there makes it all feel very real.

Allow a couple of hours inside, a little longer if you're catching a planetarium show. It's a good idea to visit in the morning so the kids have burnt off a bit of energy before a hike, or flip it round and save the indoor part for when the drizzle arrives.

Directly across the road sits the Palace of Holyroodhouse, the monarch's official residence in Scotland, which is open to visitors when the royals aren't in residence. Round the other side of Arthur's Seat, Duddingston village has a loch full of birdlife and the Sheep Heid Inn, one of Scotland's oldest pubs, which makes a fine stop after a walk through the park.

Footwear matters here. The paths up Arthur's Seat are steep, uneven and can be slippy after rain, so trainers with grip or walking boots are much better than fashion shoes. Take water and a layer too, as it gets breezy on the top.
Hungry after all that time travel? The Royal Mile is lined with cafés, pubs and takeaways, so a hot lunch is never far away.
